rules: Registration with general boundaries is sufficient for most registered titles.
The guide identifies boundary agreements and determined boundaries as the two main routes to greater precision.
A boundary agreement can record the agreed position of the legal boundary.
An agreement may also address maintenance of a boundary feature, which is distinct from legal-boundary position.
Legal advisers determine whether an agreement is appropriate, its form and whether registration should be requested.
A rebuttable presumption applies that a boundary agreement does not transfer land.
Doubt or uncertainty alone does not rebut the no-transfer presumption.
Where an agreed line differs from a title plan without a transfer, it must remain within the general-boundaries rule.
Where a transfer of land is established, the agreement can create an obligation to transfer the affected land.
Altering the register requires the relevant transaction, a copy of the agreement and the prescribed fee.
An accepted agreement is recorded by an entry in the property register of affected titles.
A registered chargee who did not consent may be served notice that the entry was made.
A recorded boundary agreement does not itself convert the boundary from general to determined.
Recording an agreement does not make the registrar guarantee the identified legal-boundary position.
A determined boundary shows the exact line of a registered-estate boundary under section 60.
The legislation does not define the word exact for a determined boundary.
HM Land Registry does not determine a boundary by resolving a disagreement about its exact location.
The exact line must first be identified before the register can show it as determined.
Each affected title's property register refers to the boundary as determined.
The title plan marks the general position of a determined boundary, often using lettered points.
A filed copy of the determined-boundary plan is retained to identify the exact line.
An owner may be unable to apply when evidence cannot establish the exact line.
Neighbours may jointly instruct an independent expert to identify the boundary.
An expert's award may bind the parties who agreed to be bound by it.
The exact line must be identified by a plan or by a plan with a verbal description.
The plan must show enough surrounding physical features to locate the boundary generally on the Ordnance Survey map.
All owners of land adjoining the boundary and their notice addresses must be identified.
For this process, owners include holders of a legal estate and registered chargees.
For unregistered adjoining land, documentary-title evidence is required to verify ownership.
Adjoining-land deeds must be checked for evidence placing the boundary elsewhere.
Apparent adjoining red edging can still conceal land owned by a third party, such as a drain.
Only one determined-boundary transaction is required regardless of the number of adjoining boundaries.
A fixed fee applies to a determined-boundary application.
The registrar must be satisfied that the claimed exact line is identified.
The applicant must show an arguable case for the claimed exact-line position.
The registrar must be able to identify adjoining owners and addresses for notice.
Notice is generally required unless written neighbour agreement or a court order is lodged.
The application must be cancelled when the statutory identification, arguable-case or notice tests are not met.
Pre-registration deeds may support the claimed exact line.
Statutory declarations may be used as supporting evidence.
Statements of truth or other signed statements may support the application.
A relied-on expert report should be uploaded with the application.
An expert conclusion is not conclusive for the registrar, even when it binds the instructing parties.
A non-groundless unresolved objection may be referred to the Land Registration division of the First-tier Tribunal.
A chartered land surveyor or other suitably qualified professional will normally certify the determined-boundary plan.
A boundary may be surveyed using measurements from permanent features.
A boundary may be surveyed using Ordnance Survey National Grid coordinates.
National Grid coordinates are most appropriate where permanent control features are sparse or measurements would be excessively long.
The boundary does not have to be physically marked by a fence, wall or other feature.
Where permanent ground markers are used, their positions must be shown on the determined-boundary plan.
Tree preservation information is published through order, zone and individual-tree datasets.
The tree preservation order dataset is supplied as CSV.
Zone and tree datasets may be supplied as CSV, GeoJSON, GML or GeoPackage.
Spatial datasets may share one URL or be served through OGC WFS or an ArcGIS API.
Field names may use hyphens, underscores or spaces.
Uppercase field-name characters are converted to lowercase.
The order dataset must contain at least one row for each tree preservation order.
Each order reference must be unique within the dataset.
An order reference must remain stable when the dataset is updated.
An order name may contain a name, reference, address or be blank.
The document URL identifies the authoritative order or designation notice.
The document URL may be blank after an order is revoked.
The zone dataset must contain at least one row for every protected zone.
Each zone reference must be unique within the zone dataset.
A zone reference must remain permanent across updates.
A zone display name may use a name, reference, address or blank value.
Each zone links to the reference of the tree preservation order that covers it.
Zone type is recorded as area, group or woodland.
Zone geometry is a polygon or multipolygon.
All zone polygon coordinates use WGS84.
Zone geometry in CSV is encoded as well-known text.
Zone notes are optional and may explain production or interpretation.
Zone entry-date records the date the entity was last updated.
When never updated, zone entry-date equals start-date.
Zone start-date records when the order came into force.
Zone end-date records revocation and remains blank while current.
The tree dataset must contain at least one row for each protected individual tree.
Each individual-tree reference must be unique.
The point field records the approximate centre of the tree.
Each tree must have a point or geometry.
Each tree links to the reference of the order affecting it.
Individual-tree geometry is represented as a polygon or multipolygon.
A tree record may provide both point and geometry.
A UPRN may be supplied when the tree has one.
Supplying a UPRN also requires address-text.
Supplying address-text also requires a UPRN.
The felled-date field records when a tree was felled and remains blank otherwise.
A felled tree uses felled-date rather than end-date to record that event.
The National LIDAR Programme provides 1m elevation data for all of England.
England was divided into 302 survey blocks for the programme.
Phase 1 capture was scheduled mainly in winter, approximately November through April.
Phase 1 blocks were captured between January 2017 and February 2023.
The first national capture of each block is identified as phase 1.
Repeat captures use incrementing phase numbers for the affected block.
The metadata states there is no current plan to recapture every phase-1 block on a rolling cycle.
Repeat blocks are selected according to the need for current elevation data.
Programme data is published quarterly on an ongoing basis.
Products are supplied in 5km tiles aligned to the Ordnance Survey grid.
Tile names encode survey ID, grid reference and first and last survey dates.
Surface models are supplied as GeoTIFF rasters.
Point-cloud data is supplied in LAZ format.
An index catalogue supplies survey-specific information for each tile.
The point cloud contains the discrete LIDAR returns used to create surface models.
Returns are classified into ground and low, medium and high vegetation groups.
Point-cloud vegetation and ground classification is automated.
The DSM is created from the last or only pulse returned to the sensor.
The DSM contains terrain and surface objects.
The DTM uses last-return pulses classified as ground and filters surface objects.
The programme metadata declares EPSG:27700 as its coordinate reference system.
The dataset reference period runs from 11 November 2016 to 5 May 2023.
A national coverage download is offered as a geodatabase archive.
A national coverage download is offered as GeoJSON.
A national coverage download is offered as GeoPackage.
A national coverage download is offered as shapefile.
The 1m composite DTM covers approximately 99 percent of England.
The composite terrain model has 1m spatial resolution.
Surface objects are removed with bespoke algorithms and manual editing.
The composite combines the time-stamped archive with National LIDAR Programme surveys.
For repeat surveys, the newest best-resolution source is selected.
Resampled sources use bilinear interpolation before merging.
The 2022 composite contains surveys from 6 June 2000 through 2 April 2022.
The composite is supplied as GeoTIFF in 5km National Grid tiles.
Contributing surveys state vertical accuracy of plus or minus 15cm RMSE.
The 50m grid is available in ASCII grid format.
The 50m grid is available in GML 3.2.1 Simple Features Profile level 0.
Ten-metre contours are available as Esri shapefile.
Ten-metre contours are available as GML 3.2.1.
Ten-metre contours are available as GeoPackage.
Ten-metre contours are available as MBTiles vector tiles.
The online download is available without registration.
ASCII, GML and shapefile supplies are delivered as tiled full-Great-Britain datasets.
The tiled national product contains 2,858 10km tiles.
The tiles are arranged in 55 folders representing 100km grid squares.
GeoPackage and vector-tile formats are supplied as one national flat file each.
Grid and contour data are supplied separately in compressed packages.
OS Terrain 50 provides full national coverage of Great Britain.
The product uses source data from the large-scale revision programme that updates OS MasterMap Topography Layer.
The documented full national grid supply is approximately 157MB compressed.
OS Terrain 50 is supplied annually in July.
Grid heights have been verified to 4m RMSE.
The product is maintained through an integrated three-to-five-year flying programme.
Grid height values are calculated at the centre of each pixel.
Grid creation produces neither tile overlaps nor common edge values.
Mean high and low water heights are assigned from local tide-table averages for each tile.
Tile-average tidal heights can create a small discrete step between adjacent tiles.
Contour products contain no contours between mean high and mean low water lines.
The shapefile version abbreviates propertyValue because shapefile field names are limited to ten characters.
